analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $7.25 in steps, with small-business tax breaks paid for by anti-tax-shelter rules.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan Republican-sponsored bill to raise the minimum wage to $7.25 was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on January 22, 2007 and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill raises the federal minimum wage in three steps, from $5.85 within about two months of passage to $7.25 two years later. To offset employer costs, it gives small businesses simpler cash accounting, permanent 15-year tax write-offs for restaurant and leasehold improvements, and a hiring tax credit for teen restaurant workers. It pays for those tax breaks with new penalties on tax shelters, tighter rules on corporations that moved headquarters overseas for tax purposes, and a tightened process for collecting employment taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum wage, most of them in restaurants, retail, and other service jobs, would see their hourly pay rise to $7.25 over two years. Small businesses with up to $10 million in receipts would get simpler accounting and longer write-offs, and restaurant employers would get a tax credit for hiring 16-to-20-year-olds.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage to $5.85 within 60 days of enactment, $6.55 twelve months later, and $7.25 twenty-four months later.
Lets small businesses with gross receipts up to $10 million use cash accounting and exempts them from inventory accounting rules, reducing bookkeeping costs.
Makes permanent the 15-year straight-line write-off for qualified leasehold improvements and restaurant property, and extends the work opportunity tax credit to restaurant employees aged 16 to 20.

Pays for the tax relief by codifying the economic substance doctrine with a 40 percent penalty on transactions lacking economic substance and applying rules treating inverted corporations as domestic to transactions after March 20, 2002.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay the minimum wage, especially restaurants and small retailers, would face higher payroll costs, partially offset by the bill's tax breaks. Corporations and investors using tax-shelter transactions lacking economic substance would face a new 40 percent penalty, and companies that moved headquarters overseas after March 2002 would owe US corporate tax. Businesses with employment tax liabilities would lose the right to a pre-levy collection due process hearing.

drawbacks.text: The wage mandate raises labor costs for employers who pay at or near the minimum, an expense that falls hardest on small restaurants and retailers; the bill's tax relief only partially offsets it.
Section 213 applies the inverted-corporation rules to transactions occurring after March 20, 2002, reaching back years before the bill's introduction to tax deals that were legal when made.
Section 214 eliminates the requirement for a pre-levy collection due process hearing for taxpayers with employment tax liabilities, removing a procedural protection for those taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The wage increase is the bill's core benefit and is substantial for the lowest-paid workers, and it is paired with real offsets for small employers rather than added debt. The main honest objections are the retroactive reach of the corporate tax provision and the loss of a pre-levy hearing for employment-tax debtors; both are real costs, though they affect comparatively narrow groups. On balance the design is a conventional wage-plus-tax-relief package, and the revenue side is aimed at tax shelters rather than ordinary taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and read twice in the Senate on January 22, 2007, then referred to the Finance Committee, where it sat without any further action until that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. George Voinovich of Ohio introduced the bill for himself and Sen. John Warner on January 22, 2007.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No committee action, floor vote, or further step of any kind appears in the bill's action history for the remainder of the 110th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the same $7.25 minimum wage was enacted into law later in 2007 through different legislation, the bill's death mainly mattered for its tax provisions: small businesses never got the simplified accounting and write-offs, and corporations using economic-substance transactions or offshore reorganizations never faced the new penalties. In the record for this bill, the Finance Committee's inaction left every side where it started.

for.name: Sen. George Voinovich
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, pairing a $7.25 minimum wage increase with small-business tax relief and anti-shelter revenue provisions.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on January 22, 2007 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by two Senate Republicans, but it was never voted on in committee or on the floor, so no party split can be measured from the record.

industries.note: They would pay higher mandated wages, which is the public's gain, but the bill offsets some of that cost with a teen hiring credit and permanent 15-year write-offs for restaurant and leasehold property.

industries.industry: Small businesses with up to $10 million in receipts
industries.note: Cash accounting and exemption from inventory rules would cut their tax bookkeeping burden, with the relief paid for by anti-shelter provisions rather than by ordinary taxpayers.

industries.industry: Tax-shelter promoters and users of economic-substance transactions
industries.note: A codified economic substance doctrine with a 40 percent penalty would make purely tax-driven transactions more costly; their loss would be revenue that funds the small-business relief.

industries.industry: Corporations that relocated headquarters overseas for tax purposes (inverted corporations)
industries.note: The bill would treat certain inverted corporations as domestic, applying the rules back to transactions after March 20, 2002, ending a tax benefit for deals already completed.
